title: Misleading Beyond Visual Tricks: How People Actually Lie with Charts
screen_reason: Content analysis of 9,958 COVID-19 data-visualization tweets. The authors define misleading posts operationally as opinion tweets whose text contains a reasoning error, and Figure 6 reports, with explicit denominators, the share of opinion tweets in each stance group that contained any reasoning error (e.g. 904/954 = 94.8% of tweets opposing COVID-19 measures). That is a share of items in a sample judged misleading against researcher coding, so CONTENT. A separate verbatim share (12% of all 9,958 charts violate visualization design guidelines) is a design-guideline judgement rather than a truth judgement and is coded QUALITY.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language tweets from Twitter's global COVID-19 stream)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-skeptic opinion tweets carrying a visualization that contained any reasoning error (the paper's operational definition of a misleading post)
estimates.denominator: 954 opinion tweets whose text opposes conventional COVID-19 measures (masks, lockdowns, vaccination) or denies the existence or severity of the crisis, drawn from 9,958 manually coded COVID-19 visualization tweets
estimates.definition: the post's text was coded as containing at least one of eight reasoning errors (cherry-picking data, cherry-picking timeframe, setting an arbitrary threshold, causal inference, issues with data validity, failure to account for statistical nuance, misrepresentation of scientific studies, incorrect reading of chart)
estimates.misinfo_def: "visualizations that the public uses as the basis of opinionated conclusions that are entirely incorrect or contain significant reasoning errors"
estimates.page_loc: Figure 6, 'The results of qualitative coding by polarity of the tweets'; denominators from the same table's Total row: 'Total 517 100.0% 954 100.0% 68 100.0% 8,419 100.0%' under the column headers Support measures / Oppose measures / Alternative measures
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Codebook open-coded by the first author on 400 tweets, then refined by two authors coding 200 posts independently with iterative discussion; the finalized codebook was applied to the whole 9,958-post corpus by the first author alone. No reliability statistic is reported for the reasoning-error codes. A separate reliability test, in which four annotators rated 400 posts on a 5-point deceptiveness scale, gave Krippendorff's alpha = 0.243 (0.351 when binarised), which the authors call a very low degree of agreement and which is why they switched to coding observable tweet-text reasoning instead of rated deceptiveness.
estimates.moderator_quote: Specifically, by applying the text polarity codes (shown in Figure 3), we can distinguish between COVID-19 data visualization posts on Twitter that are neutral - such as status updates and factual observations - and posts in which the author uses the visualization as the primary basis of support for a certain argument. For the purposes of this work, we refer to the latter group as opinion tweets. ... Therefore, we consider opinion tweets that contain reasoning issues in the way the author interprets the visualization (identified using the reasoning error codes shown in Figure 3) to be misleading tweets.
estimates.notes: The denominator is a stance-selected subset (opinion tweets that oppose COVID-19 measures), not the full corpus, so within_misinfo_content is set true and the row should not be pooled as a population content-prevalence estimate. The paper never states a pooled misleading share for the whole 9,958-post corpus, and summing the three stance groups (321+904+66) would be a cross-category sum, barred by R8. Data collection ran May 2020 to September 2021; year coded 2021 (the window's midpoint and endpoint both fall in 2021).

estimates.notes: Kept because the stance split is the paper's headline analysis and its point is that reasoning errors are not confined to skeptics. The denominator is a stance-selected subset of the corpus, so this is not a population content-prevalence estimate. A reasoning error here is a flaw in the argument the tweet builds on the chart, not necessarily a false factual claim, which is why breadth is 'misleading'.

estimates.measure_type: % of all coded COVID-19 visualization tweets whose chart violates common visualization design guidelines (truncated, dual, inverted axes, area/3D encoding, uneven binning, unclear or inappropriate encoding)

estimates.definition: the chart in the post was coded as showing at least one violation of common visualization design guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: "The terms 'deceptive', 'misleading', 'lying' are typically used to describe visualizations with visual tricks, such as truncated or inverted axes, or the violation of visualization guidelines and best practices"
estimates.source_quote: About 12% of charts we analyzed violate common visualization de- sign guidelines, however, they are not typically used to support misinformation.
estimates.page_loc: Section 7 Conclusion (the hyphen inside 'de- sign' is a line break in the PDF rendering); the same figure appears in Section 4.1.3 and Section 5.1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Design-violation codes applied to all 9,958 posts by the first author using the Figure 3 codebook; judged against visualization design guidelines, not against any external truth standard; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Figure 4: Post with visualizations containing violations of common visualization design guidelines that are not identified as misleading. Importantly, we cannot state that they are unambiguously not misleading, as previous research has shown the deceptive potential of design violations.
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY, not CONTENT: a design violation is scored against design guidelines, not against a truth standard, and a chart plotting entirely accurate data can receive the label. The paper itself separates the two, saying these charts are 'not identified as misleading' and 'not typically used to support misinformation'. Excluded from prevalence; kept for the appendix as the paper's own headline number.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) No pooled misleading share exists for the full corpus. Opinion tweets are 517+954+68 of 9,958 and 'any reasoning error' is only reported within each stance group, so an overall 'X% of COVID-19 visualization tweets are misleading' number would have to be summed across categories, which R8 forbids. 2) Individual reasoning-error codes from Figure 3 (e.g. causal inference 691 = 6.9% of all posts) were NOT extracted: in this text rendering the Figure 3 table has its code labels detached from and misordered relative to its counts, so the label-to-number mapping cannot be trusted. Figure 6, by contrast, is intact and is the source used here. 3) Text-polarity shares (9.6% of all posts oppose measures, 5.2% support, 0.7% promote alternatives, 84.5% neutral) were not extracted: stance toward COVID-19 measures is not a falsity judgement. 4) The within-Figure-6 error-type rows (cherry-picking 39.8% of skeptic opinion tweets, arbitrary threshold 46.6%, causal inference 43.5%, etc.) were not given separate rows; they are components of the 'any reasoning error' row already extracted. 5) '25% of tweets with reasoning errors ... support commonly accepted methods' is a composition of the error set, not a prevalence, and is not extracted. 6) 58% of opinion-tweet visualizations being screenshots, 21% carrying annotations, and 'more than 40% of all COVID-skeptic charts are screenshots of data exploration dashboards' describe construction attributes, not falsity. 7) Comparison figures quoted from Lo et al. (57% of misleading-tagged charts having design/perception issues) are cited from elsewhere and are barred by R8. 8) The text file carries a 'DRAFT - Privileged and Confidential Prepared at the request of Counsel' watermark line mid-page and has OCR ligature/space loss throughout; quotes above are de-hyphenated and respaced from that rendering, values are unaffected.

rob.design: Twitter COVID-19 streaming endpoint (585 platform-identified hashtags/keywords), 15 May 2020 to 6 September 2021, 2.2 billion tweets; filtered to original English-language tweets with images and randomly sampled to 162.8 million; a Multinomial Naive Bayes text classifier (accuracy 0.75, precision 0.70, recall 0.71) then a fine-tuned InceptionV3 image model (accuracy 0.73, precision 0.71, recall 0.65) reduced this to 80,400 tweets; a random sample of 33,808 was manually screened, yielding 9,958 posts with relevant COVID-19 visualizations. Codebook developed by open coding of 400 posts and refined by two authors on 200 posts; the full corpus was annotated by the first author alone, with no reliability statistic reported for the final codes. The only reliability figure given is for a discarded 5-point deceptiveness rating by four annotators on 400 posts: Krippendorff's alpha = 0.243, or 0.351 binarised. No response-rate concept applies (observational platform data).
rob.item6_quote: we used the tweet text to identify deceptive charts by applying the following definition of misleading visualizations: visualizations that the public uses as the basis of opinionated conclusions that are entirely incorrect or contain significant reasoning errors.
